NBS GHS-Panel Wave4 (2018/19) shows family inheritance as the most common plot-acquisition mode (62.7% male-managed, 63.4% female-managed); Wave5 (2023/24) confirms (64.9%, 59.7%). AG-FACT-T3-W04-DIGESTIVE-ACCURACY (2026-11-09): blocks 404-416 and comparison table 431 reviewed against OpenStax, UMN College of Veterinary Medicine, Merck Vet Manual and FAO. Bile emulsifies fats but is not an enzyme; 'chyle' at block 411 should be 'chyme'. Chymosin/rennin and salivary amylase require species/age qualification. Table 431 overgeneralizes fibre/bacterial digestion and protein synthesis; horses/rabbits are hindgut fermenters and all animals synthesize body proteins. AG-FACT-T3-W04-REPRODUCTIVE-ACCURACY (2026-11-09): blocks 482, 485, 486 and 492 compared with UMN CVM Large Animal Anatomy, Merck Vet Manual, Oregon State Extension, comparative veterinary anatomy and genetics glossaries. Vas deferens leads from epididymis to pelvic urethra; sperm mature/store in epididymis; uterus masculinus is a Müllerian remnant, not sperm duct/storage. Cowper's/bulbourethral (male) and Bartholin's/greater vestibular (female) are homologous, distinct structures. Vagina length varies by species (cow 25–30cm; ewe 10–14cm; sow 10–15cm; mare 20–35cm). Bronchioles branch from bronchi; epiglottis guards laryngeal inlet. Gill rakers filter food/particles; operculum covers/protects gills and assists water pumping in bony fish. IPPC/FAO ISPM 5 defines plant quarantine as activities to prevent introduction/spread of quarantine pests; FAO IPM identifies crop rotation as a cultural measure reducing pest/disease pressure and breaking infection chains; FAO's Manual of Fumigation for Insect Control says fumigation is used to prevent/control insect infestations and remains valuable in pest-control operations; UC IPM documents reflective mulch reducing colonisation by aphids, leafhoppers, thrips and whiteflies. Generic mulch is not universally pest-controlling and may be unsuitable for some pests, but that does not make mulching categorically not a pest-control method. The stem is overbroad and has no unique defensible 'not' answer. items.implementation_reference: Implemented 2026-11-09 from synchronized master 8114b2c3ab30a56e0357184aeb4376d7f6dceb9a. Verified composite archive SHA-256 024487129a86c3a89e55293b3ad71b0dfe8b8969ea55bbc64dbfdc17565c9a3e and exact First Term DOCX member SHA-256 df1b516cdd8855d069a329d7aa627dbd0dcd3612dd10d254c53af9cb93a56526. Inspected Week 3 block 195 ('Reviewing and enforcing the land use act of 1978') and Week 7 block 583 ('Government laws on land use of decree 1978 prevent individuals from owning land'). The official Gazette text (Decree No. 6 of 1978, now the Land Use Act) provides: s.1 vests land in each State in the Governor to hold in trust; s.2 divides management between Governor (urban) and local government (other land); s.5 authorises statutory rights of occupancy to any person; s.6 authorises customary rights of occupancy to any person/organisation for agricultural, residential and grazing purposes; ss.21–22 regulate assignment, mortgage, transfer of possession and sublease by approval/consent; s.24 provides for devolution of rights on death under customary law; ss.34/36 preserve pre-existing rights as deemed occupancy rights. Supreme Court of Nigeria in Ogunleye v Oni [1990] NGSC 40 recognised that pre-Act holders/occupiers under customary tenure continue to hold and enjoy rights as if customary rights of occupancy had been granted; Abioye v Yakubu [1991] NGSC 2 addressed whether the Act abolished customary land rights and recognised the continued relevance of customary interests subject to the Act. Legal conclusion: the Act removes radical/absolute freehold title from private persons and vests it in the State Governor as trustee, but does not prevent individuals, families or communities from holding statutory or customary rights of occupancy. The source's blanket wording is misleading; replace it with a precise distinction between absolute title and rights of occupancy. Updated the existing package open item detail/required_action to record the statutory finding and correction requirement; it remains blocking pending approved correction and the missing Week 8 law lesson. No source text was changed. No importer/tests run; testing remains deferred.

NBS General Household Survey-Panel Wave 4 (2018/19) reports family inheritance as the most common means of acquiring agricultural plots: 62.7% of male-managed and 63.4% of female-managed plots; the survey is nationally representative. NBS GHS-Panel Wave 5 (2023/24) confirms persistence: 64.9% of male-managed and 59.7% of female-managed plots were acquired through family inheritance; rental and purchase were much lower nationally. Therefore inheritance is the most common mode of acquisition in NBS farm-plot data, but not a standalone statutory tenure system; the legal framework is rights of occupancy under the Land Use Act, with statutory/customary distinctions. Source categories mix communal, inheritance, leasehold, free gift and state ownership, which are not mutually exclusive categories. Recommendation: retain the MCQ only after rewording 'method of land tenure' to 'mode of acquiring agricultural plots'; answer A inheritance. Verified composite archive SHA-256 024487129a86c3a89e55293b3ad71b0dfe8b8969ea55bbc64dbfdc17565c9a3e and exact First Term DOCX member SHA-256 df1b516cdd8855d069a329d7aa627dbd0dcd3612dd10d254c53af9cb93a56526. Inspected Week 10 block 878 (definition and examples of biennials) and Weekend Assignment Q2 block 922 (annual-crop exception options cotton, cowpea, yam, pepper). A biennial plant requires two growing seasons to complete its biological life cycle; vegetative growth typically occurs in the first season and flowering/seed production in the second. FAO EcoCrop classifies onion (Allium cepa) and carrot (Daucus carota) as biennial; onions are normally grown as annuals for bulbs and require two seasons to produce seed, and carrots normally grown as annuals for roots but may flower in the second year. FAO EcoCrop classifies cassava as a short-lived perennial (6-24 months), ginger as perennial usually grown as annual, Capsicum annuum as annual, cotton as annual/perennial but usually cultivated as annual, and cowpea as annual. CGIAR Genebanks says yams are annual or perennial vines but are mainly treated as annuals in cultivation. Thus the source's biennial examples (cassava, pepper, onions, carrot, ginger) are inaccurate except onion and carrot; pepper is not generally biennial. Q2's 'pepper' is species-ambiguous; if Capsicum, it is annual/usually cultivated as annual; if black pepper (Piper nigrum), it is perennial. Under production-cycle usage cotton/cowpea/yam/Capsicum pepper may all be grown as annual crops; under botanical lifespan, several vary by species and environment. There is no unique defensible exception. Recommendation: correct definition and examples, specify pepper species and whether classification is biological lifespan or cultivation cycle, and withdraw/rewrite Q2. No answer key/teacher decision presumed. No importer/tests run; testing remains deferred.
